newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: SNB continuing its balanced policy - Gehrig.
newsitem.headline: SNB continuing its balanced policy - Gehrig.

text.p: The Swiss National Bank (SNB) will maintain a balanced policy and seek to correct imbalances in the economy or currency within limits of its longer-term policy, SNB director Bruno Gehrig said.
Gehrig said in the text of a speech prepared for delivery the SNB would continue to steer a middle course between the needs of the economy and the effort to control inflation in the long-term.

"What the national bank has done in the past 18 months, and what we will continue to do, is to tread a narrow path between the demands of stabilising the economy and securing long-term price stability."
Gehrig said keeping inflation and interest rates low was the SNB's main contribution towards securing Switzerland's competitiveness as a place to do business.
"This...does not exclude using monetary policy to stabilise the economy or correct excessive currency distortions, but it sets limits on these short-term cyclical efforts," Gehrig said.

He said Swiss long-term interest rates are low compared with most other countries, and the SNB must work to keep things that way, to help the domestic economy and efforts to come to grips with the government's budget.
He said Swiss interest rates were roughly 2.00 percentage points lower, on average, compared with international levels last year.
Swiss 10-year bond yields are currently about 3.85 percent, compared with 6.60 percent for 10-year U.S. Treasury notes, and 5.80 percent for German 10-year yields.
"This interest rate advantage must be maintained, because low interest rates significantly help the process of structural adjustment and renewal," Gehrig said.
"Structural problems are not solved with a flood of money, but just the opposite," Gehrig said.

"I can think of no less favourable prerequisite for structural improvement than a scenario in which we ease excessively, only to be forced in two years into battling an unacceptable increase in inflation," he said.
This would be a battle with "rising interest rates, an inversion of the yield curve and a home-made increase in the value of the franc," he said. -- Zurich Editorial, +41 1 631 7340
